"Objective: assess the efficacy of intermittent versus continuous prophylactic treatment in bipolar disorder. Year-long follow-up to determine relapse rates and hospitalization frequency among patients with a history suggestive early warning signs, using structured clinical interviews for manic episodes (SCID-M) as diagnostic criteria; active group received monthly depot neuroleptics while control subjects were on an ad-hoc regimen of oral medication based upon prodromal symptoms. Yearly psychiatric outpatient department chart reviews showed that the intermittent treatment cohort experienced fewer hospitalizations and a lower incidence rate, with less frequent manic episodes preceding relapse compared to continuous prophylaxis.

"Objective: compare outcomes in patients treated intermittently versus continuously for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Patients randomized into two groups received either monthly depot neuroleptics or an as-needed oral regimen based on the presence of prodromal symptoms. Over a year, those receiving intermittent treatment demonstrated fewer hospitalizations and reduced severity scores using GADS; however structured assessments revealed that continuous prophylaxis was superior in maintaining social functioning.

"Objective: evaluate whether short-term versus long-acting neuroleptic agents reduce relapse rates more effectively among patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). A year-long study compared the effects of intermittent depot injections to a yearly oral regimen on MDE episodes, hospitalizations due directly or indirectly related events. Results indicated that those receiving monthly infusions experienced fewer relapses and shorter durations between acute phases.

"Objective: investigate relapse rates in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) undergoing different prophylactic treatment schedules over one year; half received depot neuroleptics at intervals determined by the emergence of prodromal symptoms, while others followed a continuous oral regimen. Chart reviews showed that intermittent administration led to fewer hospitalizations and lower OCD severity scores using Y-BOCS compared with those on constant medication.

"Objective: determine if brief versus extended prophylactic treatment impacts relapse rates in patients diagnosed post-diagnosis onset of schizophrenia over one year; half received monthly depot neuroleptics, while others were treated as symptoms presented. Findings indicated that the intermittent group had fewer hospitalizations and a lower frequency/severity rate for psychotic episodes.

"Objective: assess if brief prophylactic treatment reduces relapse rates in patients with bipolar disorder compared to continuous long-term medication over one year; half received monthly depot neuroleptics, while others followed an as-needed oral regimen based on prodromal symptoms. "Objective: To assess the efficacy of intermittent versus continuous neuroleptic prophylaxis in preventing psychotic relapse and associated morbidity among schizophrenic patients. Methodology involved a year-long, double-blind randomized trial comparing two groups; one receiving an active control (placebo) group while another received brief courses or depot injections every few months.  Results: The study found that intermittent treatment was superior to continuous administration in preventing psychotic episodes and hospitalizations over the course of 12 years.
